title: Medical Practice Marketing Plan for 2027: A One Page Template
seoTitle: Medical Practice Marketing Plan 2027: One Page Template
seoDescription: A one page 2027 marketing plan for medical practices: seven lines to fill in, review and privacy rules, and a quarterly rhythm built around open enrollment.
excerpt: Seven lines, one page: a 2027 marketing plan built for how patients now find a practice, including the growing number who ask AI tools first.
imageAlt: Doctor in a white coat writing in a notebook at a wooden desk with a tablet
imageIdea: Practice manager with a planning notebook at a clean desk.
author: The SocialDM Insights Team
bodyHtml:
Many practice marketing plans end up as a long deck nobody opens or a list of tactics with no goal. This one fits on a single page. Fill in the seven lines below, put it where your team can see it, and review it once a quarter. It is built for how patients look for care going into 2027, including the growing number who ask AI tools first.

Why plan now?

January is when insurance changes land. In states that use HealthCare.gov, open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs from November 1, 2026 through January 15, 2027, and Medicare open enrollment runs from October 15 through December 7, 2026, with changes taking effect January 1. Patients with new plans start checking which practices take their coverage. If your hours, accepted plans and locations are wrong online in January, you may never hear from them. For what to update before then, see will patients find your practice in January.

How patients look for a practice now

  • More patients ask AI. KFF found 29% of U.S. adults used AI tools or chatbots for health information or advice at least monthly in May 2026, up from 17% in June 2024. A separate Pew Research Center survey in June 2026 found 34% of U.S. adults have ever used AI chatbots for at least one of eight health reasons.
  • Reviews still carry weight. Across all local businesses, BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 97% of consumers read reviews and 74% seek reviews written in the last three months. That survey is not limited to healthcare, but recency matters to patients too.
  • Directories are often wrong. A study in JAMA of physicians listed in more than one of five national insurer directories found that only 19.4% had consistent address and specialty information across all of them. In our view, errors like these can mislead patients and any AI tool that draws on public listings.

For the full patient journey, see how patients choose a doctor online.

The one page template

LineWhat to write
1. GoalOne number for 2027, such as new patient appointments per month for a specific service
2. Patients we wantThe services, plans and neighborhoods you want more of, and the ones you are full on
3. Where they lookGoogle search and maps, your website, insurer directories, review sites, AI tools and referring doctors
4. Facts that must matchPractice and provider names, addresses, phone, hours, accepted plans, accepting new patients status, telehealth
5. ReviewsWho asks, when, and who replies, following the rules below
6. ContentA few pages or posts that answer what patients ask before booking
7. Numbers to check monthlyCalls, appointment requests, direction requests, review count and recency, and how AI tools describe you

Line 4: the line we would fix first

In our view, accuracy is the highest return item on the page. A patient who sees the wrong hours or an old address on a directory may not call to check. Make your website the clearest source of truth, keep your Google Business Profile current, and update insurer directories when anything changes. For how AI assistants use these facts, see will ChatGPT recommend your practice.

Line 5: review rules every practice should follow

  • Ask every patient, or none. Google's policies do not allow discouraging negative reviews or asking only happy patients, and they do not allow incentives for reviews.
  • Protect privacy in replies. Never confirm someone is a patient or mention their care in a public reply. In 2019 HHS announced a $10,000 settlement with a Dallas dental practice over patient information disclosed in responses to online reviews.
  • Reply in general terms. Thank the reviewer and invite them to contact the office directly.

This is general information, not legal advice. Check your review process with your compliance lead.

Line 6: content that earns its place

Our advice is to write for the questions your front desk hears most: which plans you take, whether you see new patients, what a first visit involves, and how soon someone can be seen. A few accurate, specific pages beat a busy blog that says little.

A quarterly rhythm from December

  1. December: Fill in the page. Check line 4 facts on your website, Google profile and the insurer directories you are listed in. Record calls, appointment requests and review count as your baseline.
  2. January to March: Watch new patient calls as HealthCare.gov open enrollment ends January 15, 2027. Start the review routine.
  3. April: Compare to the baseline, recheck line 4, and adjust line 6.
  4. July and October: Repeat the check, and plan for the next open enrollment season.

For how to size the budget behind this plan, see what the 2027 budget research actually says. If you would like help seeing where your practice shows up today on Google, maps and AI answers, see our work for medical practices or talk to our team.

Revisit in 2027: we will update these figures when KFF, Pew and BrightLocal publish new editions.

Questions we hear

What should a medical practice marketing plan include?

A clear goal, the patients you want more of, where those patients look, the facts that must be accurate everywhere, a compliant review routine, a small amount of useful content and a short list of numbers to check each month.

Can we ask every patient for a Google review?

Yes, and asking every patient is the safe approach. Google's policies do not allow incentives for reviews or asking only happy patients. Never offer anything in return for a review.

How should we reply to patient reviews?

Thank people in general terms and invite them to contact the office directly. Never confirm that someone is a patient or mention their care, even if they shared details first. In 2019, HHS announced a settlement with a dental practice over patient details disclosed in review replies.

Do patients really use AI to find health information?

Many do. KFF found 29% of U.S. adults used AI tools or chatbots for health information or advice at least monthly in May 2026, up from 17% in June 2024. In our view, that makes accurate practice details across the web more important.

When should we start the 2027 plan?

In December. HealthCare.gov open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs through January 15, 2027, so many patients will be checking whether practices take their new plan in January.
takeaways: A useful practice plan fits on one page: goal, patients, where they look, facts that must match, reviews, content and monthly numbers.
HealthCare.gov open enrollment for 2027 coverage runs through January 15, 2027, so accurate plan and hours details matter most in January.
KFF found 29% of U.S. adults used AI tools for health information at least monthly in May 2026, up from 17% in June 2024.
Ask every patient for reviews, never offer incentives, and never confirm someone is a patient in a public reply.
